1.note: These **cubits** were a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express these measurements in modern units, either in the text or a footnote. Alternate translation: [about 27 meters. Its width {was} about 2.7 meters]
The word **Dura** is the name of a plain.

2.note: These **satraps** were provincial governors of the highest rank in the Babylonian Empire. If your readers would not be familiar with what satraps were, you could use the name of a similar kind of official that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the highest provincial officials]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dedication**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to dedicate the statue]

4.note: Daniel is using **called out in strength** as a common expression of the culture to mean “loudly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [called out with a loud voice]
The pronoun **One** refers to King Nebuchadnezzar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [King Nebuchadnezzar is commanding you]

Here, **languages** represents the people who speak those languages. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [peoples, nations, and speakers of every language]

5.note: A **trigon**, a **harp**, and a **bagpipe** were kinds of musical instruments. If your readers would not be familiar with what these instruments were, you could use the names of similar instruments that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [two kinds of stringed instruments and a wind instrument]

By **fall down and worship**, the herald means to lie facedown on the ground as an act of worship. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you shall bow down to the ground and worship]

6.note: The herald is not referring to a specific person with the phrase **who that does not fall down and worship**. He means anyone at all who does not do this. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But anyone at all who does not fall down and worship]

The expression **he will be thrown** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the king’s officials will throw him into the midst of a furnace of blazing fire]

7.note: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the author is using it to indicate that follows is the result of what he has just described. Alternate translation: [As a result]

Some ancient manuscripts do not include the term “bagpipe” at the end of the list of instruments here. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts include the term, as in verses 5, 10, and 15. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

8.note: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the author is using it to indicate that follows is the result of what he has just described. Alternate translation: [Consequently]

Daniel is using the phrase **men, Chaldeans** to introduce a group of Chaldeans as new participants in the story. If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation. Alternate translation: [certain Chaldeans]

The author is using **ate the pieces of the Jews** as a common expression of the culture to mean “brought malicious accusations against the Jews.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and brought malicious accusations against the Jews] or [and maliciously accused the Jews]

9.note: The Chaldeans had not been asked a question, but Daniel uses the expression **They answered and were saying** to introduce their speech. Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The Chaldeans are using **live to eternities** as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live for a very long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live many years]

12.note: The Chaldeans are identifying Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego as Jews. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [certain Jews]

The Chaldeans are using **do not set regard on you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not respect you” or “do not obey you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [These men do not respect you] or [These men do not obey you]

13.note: The terms **rage** and **heat** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [in furious anger]

15.q: תִּפְּל֣וּן וְ⁠תִסְגְּדוּן֮ לְ⁠צַלְמָ֣⁠א דִֽי־עַבְדֵת֒ וְ⁠הֵן֙ לָ֣א תִסְגְּד֔וּן
15.note: Nebuchadnezzar is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you fall down and worship the statue that I have made, then I will not punish you for not doing this before; but if you do not worship]

Nebuchadnezzar is using the question form to assert that no god will be able to rescue Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from his power. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And there is no god who will deliver you from my hand!]

Here, **my hand** represents Nebuchadnezzar’s power to punish them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my control]

17.note: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are using **If it is** as a common expression of the culture to mean “if that happens,” referring to their being thrown into the furnace. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If we are thrown into the furnace] or [If that is what happens]
Here, **your hand** represents the king’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your control]

18.note: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [But if he does not deliver us]

The expression **may it be known to you** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you should know]

19.note: Daniel is using **was filled {with} heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean “became furious.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [became furious]

Daniel is using **one seven more** as a common expression of the culture to mean “seven times hotter” than it was usually heated. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [seven times hotter]

Daniel is using the phrase **than had been seen to heat it** as a common expression of the culture to mean “more than it had ever been heated before.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [than it had ever been heated before]

The expression **had been seen** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [than anyone had seen anyone heat it]
Here, **seven** might not be an exact number. It may represent completion. Alternate translation: [as many times hotter as possible, hotter than it had ever been heated before]

20.note: The author is using the expression **men, men of valor** to introduce these new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [certain men of valor] or [certain strong soldiers]

21.note: The term that the ULT translates as **tunics** refers to some kind of inner garment that people of this culture wore under their **cloaks**. Some interpreters understand it to mean “trousers.” However, since the exact meaning is uncertain, you may wish to use a general phrase in your translation. Alternate translation: [their inner garments]

22.note: The author is using **All before this** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of this” or “on account of this.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Because of this] or [For this reason]

25.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **appearance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the fourth one]

Nebuchadnezzar is using **a son of the gods** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a god.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a god]

26.note: It might seem that saying **his** in addition to the possessive phrase with **of** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can shorten this expression. Alternate translation: [servants of the Most High God]

27.note: Daniel is speaking of **the fire** as if it were a living thing that could rule over the men’s bodies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the fire had not damaged their bodies]

28.q: בְּרִ֤יךְ אֱלָהֲ⁠הוֹן֙ דִּֽי־שַׁדְרַ֤ךְ מֵישַׁךְ֙ וַ⁠עֲבֵ֣ד נְג֔וֹ
28.note: Nebuchadnezzar is praising God when he says **Blessed {be} the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego**. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as an expression of praise or blessing in your language. You might express this as a declaration of praise, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be praised]

Nebuchadnezzar is using **gave up their bodies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “were willing to die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and were willing to die]

29.note: The expression **And from me a decree is set** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I am setting forth this decree]

The phrase **anything** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction, “anything wrong,” in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area.

The expressions **will be made {into} limbs** and **its house be made a rubbish heap** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will have my soldiers cut them into limbs and make their house a rubbish heap]

Nebuchadnezzar is using **will be made {into} limbs** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be cut into pieces.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be cut into pieces]

Nebuchadnezzar is using **all before that** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [seeing that] or [because]

Nebuchadnezzar is speaking as if the offender’s house were **a rubbish heap**. He means that it will be completely destroyed and reduced to ruins. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and its house be completely destroyed]
